sentences.text: Uktenadactylus is an extinct pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous found in the Paw Paw Formation of Texas, USA, and the Isle of Wight, southern England.
The holotype specimen is a partial snout about fifteen centimetres long, consisting of the premaxilla and a small part of the maxilla.
The fossil preserves the base of a crest that curves upwards to a height of 7.5 cm and a thickness of 4 mm.
The snout shows eight tooth sockets on the left side and six on the right side.
The third pair of teeth is the largest, with a diameter of approximately 17.6 to 17.7 mm, while the sockets increase in size from the tip backward.
The first pair of teeth was located on the flattened tip of the snout, pointing forward.
A crest on the base curves upward to a height of 7.5 centimeters with a thickness of four millimeters at that point.
The genus name derives from Uktena, a horned giant snake from Cherokee mythology, and the Greek term daktylos, meaning "finger," referring to the typical wing finger common in pterosaur names.
The genus contains only one species, Uktenadactylus wadleighi, which is known from a single partial snout fossil originally assigned to the genus Coloborhynchus.

In 2009, paleontologists Taissa Rodrigues and Alexander Kellner created the new genus Uktenadactylus for the species C. wadleighi after concluding that the genus Coloborhynchus contained only one species.
In 2020, a second species, U. rodriguesae, was named based on a snout fragment found on the Isle of Wight, though a debate exists regarding this jaw fragment.
Researchers conclude that Uktenadactylus, Coloborhynchus clavirostris, and Siroccopteryx likely formed an unnamed clade within the family Anhangueridae.
Many analyses, including those in 2020, place Uktenadactylus within the family Anhangueridae and the subfamily Coloborhynchinae.
A 2020 analysis by Holgado and Pêgas recovered Uktenadactylus as the sister taxon of Nicorhynchus within the subfamily Coloborhynchinae.
Uktenadactylus is classified as a reptile.
Uktenadactylus lived from the Barremian to the Albian stages, between 125.77 and 100.5 million years ago.

Rodrigues and Kellner based their distinction between Uktenadactylus and Coloborhynchus clavirostris on stratigraphic, methodological, and phylogenetic considerations, yet there is a debate regarding a jaw fragment from the Isle of Wight; while Martill (2015) assigned it to Coloborhynchus, Holgado and Pêgas (2020) described it as a new species of Uktenadactylus, U. rodriguesae.
